---
name: headless-blender-iteration-workflow
description: "How Luka wants Blender experiments iterated autonomously (Fable folder, versioned scripts + renders, Blender 4.3 path, conversation archived)"
metadata: 
  node_type: memory
  type: feedback
  originSessionId: 3e5dff24-aabb-4241-b30f-ec038bf50948
  modified: 2026-08-20T20:42:40.715Z
---

For "redo experiment N with the new workflow" requests: outputs go in `experiments/<N>/Fable/`,
each iteration saved as `experiment_NN_fable_vXX.py` + `experiment_NN_fable_vXX_blender_view_YY.png`
(mirrors the `ChatGPT 5.1/` folder naming), rendered headless with Blender 4.3 at
`C:/Program Files/Blender Foundation/Blender 4.3/blender.exe` (5.1 also installed, untested).
Renders must be shaded with object outlines on (coplanar pieces distinguishable); add close-up /
layer-hidden views freely. Max 10 model iterations; minimise questions; consult `input/` manuals
for construction questions; archive the session transcript (copy the `.jsonl` into the folder).

**Why:** Luka works as architect/reviewer and wants to compare LLM runs side by side with the
earlier ChatGPT workflow, including the full conversation.

**How to apply:** Reuse `experiments/13_.../Fable/render_fable.py` as the renderer template; pass an
absolute output prefix (Blender resolves relative paths against its own cwd). See
[[craftbot-project-overview]] if it exists.

Since experiment 02 (2026-08-22) `render_fable.py` also runs a SAT box-box overlap check after rendering (prints penetrating pairs > 1 mm); reuse `experiments/02_Carport_Gothic_Blender_Python/Fable/render_fable.py` when the model is all `place_element` boxes — it catches joint errors the renders hide.

Experiment 03 (2026-08-22): `experiments/03_VIPP_Shelter_Blender_Python/Fable/` has the most general versions of the helpers (`get_collection` nested paths, `box()` from corner coords, `stud_wall` with door/window openings + noggins, `tile_sheets`/`clad_x` plywood tiling) and a renderer with the SAT check — start new box-only experiments from there. Heredocs containing apostrophes break the Bash tool on Windows; use the Write tool for scripts.

Experiment 04 (2026-08-22): `experiments/04_Construction_Manual_Blender_Python/Fable/` adds `prism()` / `prism_x()`
(convex prisms from a 2D profile) + `clip()`/`strip()` half-plane clipping for trusses, purlins, sheets, stringers, and a
`render_fable.py` whose overlap check is a generic convex-mesh SAT (works for boxes *and* prisms). Start from there for any
model with sloped members; rotated boxes cannot be plumb/mitre cut and always fail the overlap check at joints.
Phase-2 pattern (exp 04, 2026-08-23): after the first clean model Luka asks to compare it with the *photos/drawings* in
the source PDF (read the PDF pages with Read, not just the extracted .md — the appendix sheets carry the plan and
panel dimensions), list differences + independent structural improvements, then iterate again. Expect a rationale
with extra sections (reference comparison, structural improvements).

Experiment 06 (2026-08-23): `experiments/06_Prouve_Cabanon_Blender_Python/Fable/` adds `prism_y` (x-z profile along Y),
`split_rows` + `panel_end`/`panel_side` wall-infill generators (rows x columns with holes, top clipped by a roof plane),
lattice legs from `strip`+`clip` (consecutive diagonals need a node offset >= width/sin(angle) or the SAT check flags them),
and bevelled ridge/rail tops defined by one `z_u(y)` roof-plane function. Always render frame-only views first: the SAT check
cannot detect *missing* geometry (v01 had the portico clipped away by a sign error and still reported 0 overlaps).

Experiment 07 (2026-08-23): `experiments/07_Gehry_Deconstruction_Blender_Python/Fable/` adds the most general toolkit:
`Frame` + `frame_prism` (polygon in any plane, extruded, cut by 3D half-spaces), `slab_coeffs` (thickness-exact clipping),

content.content:
ORIGINAL PROMPT


Here is a PDF that describes construction principles for a Canadian wood-frame house, specifically chapters on roof construction and sheathing. I want you to do the following:

1. Please read the manual I gave you and familiarize yourself with the principles of constructing a timber frame roof.

2. Describe step-by-step a way to construct a hip roof using timber frame construction.

3. Translate this construction process into a Python code that can generate the same structure in Blender. Use two Python files I gave you as a reference. Use the place_element() function from craftbot_lib.py to build the geometry - element_placement_template.py is just an example script that shows how this could be done.




____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. I want you to do the following:

1. Make the roof longer in the X direction. This will give us space to add other elements to it later.
2. Add jack rafters to all sides of the building.
3. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Good progress. Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. I want you to do the following:

1. Add the "king rafter" on each side of the roof - connecting ridge with the plate board.
2. Add ceiling joists across the building.
3. Increase the steepness / height of the roof.
4. Add another roof wing connecting to this one forming a T roof structure on the south side.
5. Add a dormer window on the north side of the roof. Use the image in the PDF manual on page 11 as a reference.
6. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Analyze them and determine geometric mistakes. Then, let's do the following:

1. The south T-wing is rotated 90 degrees from how it should be. Rotate it correctly and connect it to the existing roof. Make sure to model valley rafters and valley jack rafters correctly at the intersection of two roof wings.
2. Remove current ceiling joists and add those that span the shorter side of the roof (Y direction).
3. Dormer window on the north side is completely wrong. Please consult the window_dormer_diagram.png, study the listed terms and make a plan on how to construct it before you proceed with the code.
4. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Then, let's do the following:

1. Analyze the pictures and determine geometric mistakes in the dormer window. For example, dormer ridge seems to be turned 90 degrees wrong in relation to the north roof.
2. Devise a strategy to correct the dormer window and construct it according to the reference diagram from the PDF document (attached to this prompt).
3. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Dormer window is still wrong, let's focus on getting that right. I attached a photo of a dormer window from outside that we can use as a reference, your generated model looks nothing like that. Analyze the pictures and determine geometric mistakes in the dormer window from your code, then implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Dormer window is still wrong, let's focus on getting that right:

1. Rotate Dormer_Ridge, Dormer_Plate_Front and Dormer_Plate_Back elements 90 degrees around the Z axis, then adjust dormer rafters and other elements accordingly.
2. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.

 


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's focus on getting the dormer window right:

1. Dormer_Ridge, Dormer_Plate_Front and Dormer_Plate_Back are now all at the same height. Make Dormer_Ridge higher so to create a sloped roof of the dormer window.
2. Add vertical side studs between the roof rafter and dormer plate elements.
3. Currently, Dormer_Valley_Jack and Dormer_Valley elements are in a wrong place. They should be connecting dormer plates with the dormer ridge and the ridge board of the large roof. Check and correct element connectivity.
4. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's focus on getting the dormer window right. The file experiment_12_chatgpt51_v10.py contains the correct Blender Python code to generate a dormer window. Go through it and use it to generate the correct dormer window geometry in our code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.

 

____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT

Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. It looks like we made some progress on the dormer window by integrating the code from the other file, but we need to do more adjustments. Let's do the following.

1. New dormer window is too big for the current roof. Make the large roof larger in size (about 1.5x scale factor) so the dormer window fits. Make sure to trim the roof rafters under the dormer (see diagram).
2. Extend Wing_Ridge in +Y direction until it connects with the Ridge_Board.
3. Add jack rafters on the roof wing - between Wing_Ridge and Valley_W and Valley_E respectively.
4. Remove elements Rafter_S_01 to Rafter_S_09, they seem to not be needed anymore as we already have trimmed rafters that replace them.
5. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. Make sure the rafters on the north side of the large roof match the spacing from the rafters on the south side. Scale the dormer window if needed.
2. Align the dormer window with the roof rafters underneath. Make dormer side studs land on the roof rafters below.
3. Roof rafters that sit between the two rafters supporting the dormer should be trimmed in the middle of their length so they form a gap beneath the dormer. Upper side should run from the roof ridge to the dormer valley rafters. The lower side should run from the Plate_Long_N to the double header beam below the window - add that one in as well, it should mirror the Dormer_DoubleHeader element but be below the dormer window.
4. Extend Wing_Ridge in +Y direction until it hits the point where Valley_W and Valley_E cross.
5. Add one more valley jack rafter between Valley_Jack_W_01 and Valley_Jack_E_01 that extends from the roof ridge to the Wing_Ridge (which will now be extended to that point on the roof).
6. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. In this version of the code the spacing of the dormer rafters suddenly changed, it seems it got more spaced out and uneven. Switch it back to what we had before, a more even and slightly denser arrangement.
2. Remove Dormer_LowerHeader_A and Dormer_LowerHeader_B, and extend Dormer_TrimmedBottom_0 and Dormer_TrimmedBottom_1 to the Dormer_FrontSupportBeam.
3. Add ceiling joist elements on the roof wing running in west-east direction.
4. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.


____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. Clean up the dormer window framing - remove Dormer_TopPlate_FB_0, Dormer_Window_Header, Dormer_Window_Jamb_0/1,Dormer_Window_Sill.
2. Add top braces to Dormer_Valley_Jack elements (similar as we did with Dormer_Rafter elements).
3. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. Create two more dormer windows, one on either side of the current one on the north roof side. Make sure to have an even spacing of rafters throughout.
2. Roof rafters that directly support the dormer window (studs come on top of them) should be doubled. Just place another rafter right next to it.
3. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. Space the three dormer windows slightly apart with two roof rafters in between.
2. New dormer valley top braces should be shifted in the -Y direction for one profile thickness to avoid overlap. Also, scale their lengths down approx. 0.6x, this will make them match closer the other top braces.
3. Don't forget to add Dormer_TrimmedTop elements above each dormer window like we had before.
4. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. Dormer windows are now correctly spaced, but the roof rafter in between are missing. Add one rafter in between the dormer windows.
2. We are missing some Dormer_TrimmedTop and Dormer_TrimmedBottom elements - D2_Dormer_TrimmedTop_0, D2_Dormer_TrimmedBottom_0, D0_Dormer_TrimmedTop_1 and D0_Dormer_TrimmedBottom_1 are all missing, please add them in.
3. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.



____________________________


FOLLOW UP IN THE SAME CONTEXT / CHAT


Here are the screenshots of the Blender model generated for your reference. Let's do the following:

1. Turn the roof wing into a hip roof. Add the roof inclination on the south side, hip rafters and jack rafters etc.
2. Fix the alignment of jack rafters on both sides of Hip_NW and Hip_SW. The alignment is perfect on the east side of the roof so you can use that as a reference. It seems the jack rafters on the north and south side of the large hip roof need to be shifted, and the jack rafters on the west hip roof stay the same.
3. Implement these improvements into the Blender Python code. Use the already generated code as a reference. Write out the entire code in copy-paste ready form.

## Roof slope conventions (p. 118–119)

- Slope = rise-to-run ratio, **rise always first**. Two conventions:
  - **Imperial:** run always 12 (framing square). 45° = 12/12; 4/12 = 4 in. rise per 12 in. run.
  - **Ratio:** for slopes < 45° the *first* number (vertical) is 1 (e.g. 1:5 = 1 vertical per 5 horizontal); for slopes > 45° the *second* number (horizontal) is 1 (e.g. 5:1). Avoid mixed units (1 mm in 10 m).
  - 4/12 ≡ 1:3. Angular expressions acceptable where high accuracy needed.
- Pitched roofs vary from **1:6 to 1:1 or more**. Minimum slope for asphalt shingles is 1:6; different installation rules for ≥ 1:3 and < 1:3.
- Roof must have water-shedding surface, air and vapour barriers, thermal insulation and ventilation. Most Canadian houses: prefabricated trusses + unheated ventilated attic. Cathedral ceilings and flat roofs still need a vented space above insulation.
- Roof joist/rafter sizes by species/grade/live load: Tables 29–32 (pp. 295–301, not in excerpt).

## Chapter 11 — Ceiling and Roof Framing

### Pitched roofs (p. 119)
- Prefabricated trusses most often used; site-framed rafters sometimes. **Gable roof is simplest**; hip or L-shape roofs can also be trussed (**Fig. 77**: L-shape trussed roof — plan with hatched roof planes and a valley; isometric shows ridge, valley trusses, roof sheathing, gable end, girder truss, common trusses, double wall plates).

### Prefabricated roof trusses (pp. 119–122)
- Advantages: designed for local snow loads, quality control, less lumber waste, faster enclosure; provide surface for sheathing and ceiling, space for insulation.
- **Raised heel trusses** (**Fig. 78**) used in most new houses — deeper space at the eaves for insulation; truss anchors as requested by manufacturer/code. Energy codes lead to vertical depth ≥ 300 mm (12 in.) at outer face of exterior wall for trusses, rafters and roof joists.
- Trusses typically span exterior wall to exterior wall, no intermediate bearing → partitions placed freely; continuous air barrier/vapour retarder applied to underside before partitions.
- **Fig. 79 — Types of prefabricated roof trusses:** king-post · Howe · Fink or W · mono-pitch · parallel chord · scissor truss · mansard.
- Storage flat and clean; spans < 6 m (20 ft) installed by hand, longer need lifting equipment. Lift vertically to avoid lateral bending.
- Erection: gable truss first, braced to ground and wall; each additional truss generally **600 mm (24 in.) o.c.**, toe-nailed to top plates, temporarily braced (**Fig. 80** — gable ends normally sheathed before end braces). Then permanent bracing (**Fig. 81**): (a) top chord plane, (b) lateral web bracing, (c) web/bottom chord plane. Plan view: lateral braces across top chords, diagonal brace nailed to web repeated at ~6 m (20 ft); end elevation: 38 × 89 mm web bracing; side elevation: sheathing, blocking, lateral brace, diagonal braced bay at both ends and ~6 m intervals. Sheathing adds stiffness. Do not cut or alter trusses.

### Site assembly of pitched roofs (pp. 122–127)

**Fig. 82 — Types of pitched roofs:** Flat · Monopitch · Gable · Hip · Gambrel · Mansard.

- Gable roof: rafters/trusses same length and pattern. Dormers add light/headroom (Fig. 88). **Hip roof: common rafters fastened to a ridge board, hip rafters supporting the jack rafters (Fig. 83B).**
- Liveable attics need insulation, air barrier, vapour barrier; framing may need to be upsized for insulation depth.
- **Ceiling joists** support ceiling finish and act as ties between exterior walls / opposing rafters; may carry loads from dwarf (knee) walls → size accordingly (Table 33); if they carry floor loads use floor joist tables (Tables 19, 20).
- Nail ceiling joists **after wall framing, before rafters** (rafter thrust otherwise pushes walls out). Joists tie lower ends of rafters in roofs sloping **≥ 1:3**; nail ceiling joist to side of each pair of rafters (**Fig. 83**).
- **Hip roofs:** where jack rafters run perpendicular to ceiling joists, a **stub joist** ties the jack rafter back to the ceiling joist (**Fig. 85**). Lap and nail joists or splice at centre bearing wall for a continuous tie. Nail counts depend on slope, spacing, snow load, house width (Table 24).

**Fig. 83 — Roof framing and attachment**
- **A Gable roof:** ridge board, rafter, collar brace, collar tie, gable end stud, ceiling joist, top wall plate.
- **B Hip roof:** hip rafter **at least 50 mm (2 in.) deeper than jack rafters**, jack rafter, ceiling joist, top plate. Isometric: four hip rafters rising from the corners to a short ridge (shown as a vertical post marker at the apex in the drawing), jack rafters from plates to hips, common rafters from plates to ridge, ceiling joists spanning the short direction.

- Dwarf walls perpendicular to ceiling joists (**Fig. 84**) add roof load; increase joist depth one size when slope > 1:4; when ≤ 1:4 use roof joist tables.
- **Fig. 84 — Rafter heel supported on a rafter plate:** rafter plate nailed to top of each ceiling joist with ≥ two 100 mm (4 in.) nails; rafter; ridge beam; exterior wall; knee wall with top and bottom plates and stud in line with each ceiling joist and rafter; struts at 1.2 m (4 ft) o.c.; ceiling joists lapped directly above interior load-bearing wall.
- Hip rafters ~51 mm (2 in.) deeper than common/jack rafters reduce space along end walls; in low-slope roofs the outside ceiling joist may not fit at normal spacing → **doubled joists** positioned to suit, then **tail joists** toenailed to outside wall plate and end-nailed to the doubled joist, at the same spacing as main joists (**Fig. 85**: jack rafter, hip rafter ≥ 50 mm deeper, ceiling joist, double ceiling joist, normal location for ceiling joist if space available, stub joist, end wall framing top plate).
- **Cutting rafters:** proper angle at ridge; **bird's mouth** notches at eaves; heel bears directly over exterior wall. Rafters placed: (a) directly on wall plates (Fig. 83); (b) on a rafter plate on the ceiling joists (Fig. 84); (c) on a load-bearing wall supported on the exterior wall plate (**Fig. 86**, used where part of the outside wall is inset — ceiling joists extend beyond exterior wall and are nailed to rafter sides).
- **Ridge board or ridge beam** ensures a level ridgeline. Erect rafters in pairs, nail to ridge, toe-nail lower ends to wall plate. Pairs directly opposite or **offset at ridge by ≤ their thickness** (offset needed when joists are lapped at the centre wall).
- **Slope < 1:3 → vertical support at peak:** 38 × 140 mm (2 × 6) ridge beam supported at 1.2 m (4 ft) by 38 × 89 mm (2 × 4) struts, or a load-bearing wall. Ridge support eliminates outward thrust → continuous ties unnecessary. Ridge beams also needed on steep roofs where rafter ends can't be tied.
- **Intermediate support** between ridge and exterior walls reduces rafter span (span measured from intermediate point to ridge/eave):
  - Slope ≥ 1:3: 38 × 89 mm **collar ties** nailed to each rafter pair; ties > 2.4 m (8 ft) braced against buckling with a 19 × 89 mm continuous member at right angles near centre (three 76 mm nails each end).
  - Slope < 1:3: **dwarf bearing wall** (Fig. 84), single top plate allowed if rafters over studs.
  - **Struts** 38 × 89 mm nailed to rafter side, bearing on load-bearing partition, **≥ 45° from horizontal** (Fig. 86).
  - Rafters perpendicular to ceiling joists: dwarf wall on a **beam between ceiling joists**, beam underside ≥ 25 mm (1 in.) above ceiling finish via blocks at bearing points.
  - Hip/valley rafters: beam with roof strut; or for a few rafters at a hip end a **"strongback"** of two 38 × 89 mm nailed on edge under the rafters, supported by 38 × 89 mm struts radiating from a common point on the interior bearing wall.
- **Hip and valley rafters ~50 mm (2 in.) deeper than common rafters** → full contact with the angle-cut of jack rafters (Figs. 83, 85, 87). Hip roof: jack rafters nailed to hip rafters and wall plate. Valley: jack rafters nailed to valley rafter and ridge.
- **Fig. 86 — Rafter heel supported on load-bearing wall:** ridge board; intermediate struts ≥ 45° to horizontal; 38 mm (2 in.) splice plate; interior bearing wall; rafters notched and bearing on top plate of exterior wall; continuous nailer and soffit supports; ceiling joists extend beyond exterior wall, nailed to rafters and toe-nailed to double wall plate; studs in load-bearing wall directly under each rafter; wall sheathing; exterior wall. Inset shows a house with an inset wall portion.
- **Fig. 87 — Framing at a valley:** valley rafter, jack rafter, common rafter, top plate, corner wall studs (inside corner of an L-plan: valley rafter rises from the inside corner; jack rafters from each wing's plate to the valley).
- **Dormers (Fig. 88):** rafters each side **doubled** to support side studs and valley rafters; top ends of valley rafters on a **double header** between the doubled rafters (joist hangers). Usual method: install roof sheathing first, frame dormer, cut sheathing flush with framing around opening; **bottom plate on top of the sheathing** supports side studs and is nailing base for wall sheathing. Size window for flashing/detailing.

### Gable-end framing and projections (pp. 127–129)
- After roof framing, nail **gable-end studs**; in unfinished attics wide face may be parallel to wall; cut to rafter angle, toenail to plate and rafter underside with ≥ four 63 mm (2½ in.) nails each end.
- **Projection < 300 mm (12 in.)** (**Fig. 90 — Narrow projection**): **rake rafter** supported by ridge beam, rafter header, blocking and sheathing; 19 mm (¾ in.) nailing strip fastened to rafter above gable wall; blocking 600 mm (24 in.) o.c. toenailed to strip, end-nailed to rake rafter; soffit nailed to these, fascia added; gable wall sheathing taken up to underside of roof sheathing; rough fascia supports heel of rake rafter.
- **Projection > 300 mm (12 in.)** (**Fig. 89 — Wide projection supported by "lookout" rafters**): gable-end studs with narrow face parallel to sheathing + top wall plate; **lookouts** same size as rafters, **600 mm (24 in.) o.c.**, end-nailed to the first rafter inboard and to the gable top plate; blocking between lookouts at the wall line supports sheathing and inner soffit edge; **lookout length ≥ 2 × overhang**; **double rafter** where lookouts project > 1.5 rafter spaces into the roof. Labels: ridge beam, rafter, top plate of gable end wall, blocking between lookouts, lookouts 600 mm o.c., ceiling joist, top plate, header or rough fascia, fascia board at eave and gable end, corner studs.

### Low-slope roofs (pp. 129–130)
- Must be more watertight (poorer drainage); may carry decks/traffic → durable materials.
- Rafters doubling as ceiling joists = **"roof joists"**, sized for roof + ceiling loads (Tables 29, 30); may need wider lumber / engineered wood for insulation and ventilation depth.
- Laid level or nearly level; **slope ≥ 1:50 for drainage** via ledger strip on bearing wall or tapered strip on joists.
- Overhang via **lookout rafters** (**Fig. 91**): if projecting > 1.5 joist spaces, two roof joists nailed together form a header; outside rafter header end-nailed to lookouts and joists (nailing for sheathing, fascia, soffit). Labels: alternative framing layout (dashed), roof joist, lookout rafter, header, exterior wall plate, rafter header.

### Roof space ventilation (pp. 130–131)
- Always ventilate above insulation; membranes are vapour-resistant so vapour must be removed by ventilation.
- **Ice dams:** heat loss + sun melts roof snow, refreezes on cold eaves → water backs up (Fig. 100). Airtightness + insulation + ventilation keeps attic cold.
- Clearance between insulation and sheathing: **≥ 63 mm (2½ in.) without baffles, 25 mm (1 in.) with baffles**.
- **Vent area: ≥ 1/300 of insulated ceiling area for slopes ≥ 1:6; ≥ 1/150 for slopes < 1:6**; roof, gable or eave vents (**Fig. 92** soffit ventilation: baffle, perforated soffit, pre-finished fascia, airflow; **Fig. 93** ridge vent and gable vent). Uniformly distributed, ≥ 25% at bottom, ≥ 25% at top.
- Batt insulation between roof-ceiling joists (low slope): ≥ 63 mm vent space — achievable with **38 × 64 mm (2 × 3) cross-purlins** at right angles over joists (may be shimmed for slope). Rigid insulation above sheathing → no ventilation needed.
- Vents must exclude rain, snow, insects; baffle if moisture source; corrosion-resistant metal/plastic screens.
- **Attic access hatch ≥ 0.32 m² (3.4 sq ft), no dimension < 500 mm (20 in.)** except very small attics.

### Worked sizing examples (pp. 132–134)

| Example | Conditions | Selection |
|---|---|---|
| **Ceiling joists (Fig. 94)** | Inaccessible attic, no storage; ceiling carries insulation + drywall; span 4.3 m (14 ft 2 in.); spacing 400 mm (16 in.); SPF No. 2 and better | Table 33 → **38 × 140 mm (2 × 6)** |
| **Roof rafters (Fig. 95)** | Ottawa; snow load 1.72 kPa (36 psf); slope 1:3; rafter span 4.7 m (15 ft 6 in.); SPF No. 2; shingle roofing; lower ends restrained | Table 31 → **38 × 184 mm (2 × 8) at 300 mm o.c.** or **38 × 235 mm (2 × 10) at 600 mm o.c.** |
| **Roof joists (Fig. 96)** | Ottawa; 1.72 kPa; slope 1 in 3; roof joist span 4.19 m (13 ft 9 in.); SPF No. 2; shingles; lower ends restrained | Table 29 → **38 × 235 mm (2 × 10) at 400 mm o.c.** or **38 × 286 mm (2 × 12) at 600 mm o.c.** |

Note (p. 132): National Building Code metric spacings are soft conversions — 12/16/24 in. → 300/400/600 mm; to suit 1220 × 2440 mm (4 × 8 ft) panels actual spacing is commonly **305/406/610 mm** o.c. Members must also be deep enough for required insulation.

### Sustainable housing insight — Ch. 11 (p. 135)
- Energy: raised heel trusses / deep rafters for insulation over exterior walls; consider deeper members or closer spacing for future solar panels.
- Resource: trusses use select lumber + metal plates for long spans, less wood; suit local climate; fast; space for insulation/ventilation; all roof shapes; no site cut-offs.
- Affordability: plan attic conversion — stair location, size ceiling joists as floor joists, movable insulation, steeper slopes shed snow and enclose more attic volume, rough-in services.

## Chapter 12 — Roof Sheathing and Coverings

### Roof sheathing (pp. 136–138)
- Sheathing-grade plywood, OSB or lumber planks over trusses/joists/rafters → nailing base for roofing + lateral bracing.
- **Panels (Fig. 97):** face grain **at right angles to framing**, joints offset (staggered), **2–3 mm (⅛ in.) gap**. Nails **150 mm (6 in.) o.c. minimum at edges, 300 mm (12 in.) o.c. intermediate**. Edge support: metal H-clips, 38 × 38 mm (2 × 2) blocking, or tongue-and-groove plywood. Thickness per Table 35 (depends on support spacing and edge support). Stagger fasteners at adjoining panel edges. Staples for 9.5 mm sheathing: 1.6 mm thick, 38.1 mm long, 9.5 mm crown, crown parallel to framing. Built-up roofing used as walking deck needs ≥ 15.5 mm (⅝ in.) sheathing.
- **Lumber boards (Fig. 98):** laid closed (edge to edge), ends supported, joints staggered. High wind/earthquake: laid **diagonally** or engineered. Usually 19 mm (¾ in.) thick; 17 mm allowed when supports ≤ 400 mm o.c. Boards ≤ 184 mm (8 in. nominal) wide: two 51 mm (2 in.) nails per bearing; wider: three; high wind: 63 mm nails. **No boards wider than 286 mm (12 in. nominal).** For wood shingle roofs boards may be **spaced** at the shingle exposure on centre (damp climates; lets shingles dry). Fig. 98 shows spaced method (nailing strips) above and closed method (roof boards, joint) below, on rafters/ceiling joists/plate.
- **Details (Fig. 99):** **50 mm (2 in.) clearance** of sheathing and framing from interior masonry/metal chimneys (12 mm / ½ in. for exterior masonry chimneys); header around opening; nail sheathing to rafters and headers. Fit sheathing tightly at **valleys and hips** and nail to valley/hip rafter → smooth base for flashing. Figure shows L-plan roof with valley, chimney opening with header, rafters, ridge board, ceiling joist, plate, stud.

### Eave protection (pp. 138–140)
- Membrane along roof edge against water entry. **Not required** over unheated garages/porches, slope ≥ 1:1.5, or regions ≤ 3,500 heating degree-days.
- Extends **≥ 900 mm (36 in.) up the roof** (measured along slope) to **≥ 300 mm (12 in.) inside the inner face of the exterior wall** (horizontal). Installed under shingle starter course; usually self-adhering bituminous or roll roofing membrane (type S smooth or type M mineral-surfaced roll roofing, joints lapped ≥ 100 mm and cemented; or peel-and-stick).
- **Fig. 100 — Eave protection:** top: no protection — snow, trapped water backs up through membrane, thin ice slab under snow, melted snow running down underside of sheathing, ice in eavestrough; bottom: protection directs water off the roof. Prevent ice damming by air-sealing ceiling, ceiling/wall junction, penetrations; adequate insulation; eave venting. Keep skylights away from ice-dam areas.

### Roof coverings (pp. 140–146)
- Install as soon as sheathing is on. Asphalt shingles common on pitched roofs; prefinished metal/galvanized steel/aluminum common in some regions (sheds snow); also roll roofing, wood shingles, shakes, sheet metal, concrete/clay tile; built-up with gravel/cap sheet for low slopes. Min/max slopes per covering in Table 36.
- **Minimum slopes: 1:6 asphalt shingles (low-slope application); 1:4 wood shingles; 1:3 hand-split shakes and asphalt shingles (normal application).**

#### Asphalt shingles on slopes ≥ 1:3 (**Fig. 101**)
- Min No. 210 grade; square-butt strip **310 × 915 mm (12 × 36 in.)** or **335 × 1000 mm**, three tabs, exposure **130 mm (5 in.) or 145 mm (5¾ in.)**; 21–26 strips per bundle ≈ 3 m² (32 sq ft). Store flat; distribute bundles on roof.
- Sequence: eave protection → **starter strip** (shingles with tabs removed, or reversed shingles, or type M roll roofing) projecting ≥ 12 mm (½ in.) beyond eaves, rakes and fascia (drip edge; metal drip edges also ok), nailed 300 mm o.c. → first course with butt edge in line with bottom of starter strip → subsequent courses at allowed exposure (depends on slope, shingle type/length), aligned with chalk lines or underlay print lines.
- **Four large-head roofing nails per strip**, penetrating ≥ 12 mm into sheathing. Self-sealing tar seals. Fig. 101 labels: roof sheathing, eave protection, roofing nail, tar seals, exposure, fascia board, starting course.

#### Asphalt shingles on low slopes 1:6 to 1:3
- Three thicknesses everywhere except first two courses, incl. hips and ridges; **exposure ≤ ⅓ shingle height**. Starter strips over a continuous cement band ≥ 200 mm (8 in.) wide; first course cemented with a band exposure + 100 mm (e.g. 250 mm for 150 mm exposure); subsequent courses band exposure + 50 mm (200 mm for 150 mm exposure); band 25–50 mm above butt edge to avoid defacing. Four fasteners above exposed portion. Cold cement ≈ 0.5 L/m², hot ≈ 1 kg/m². Only needed below 1:4 — special low-slope shingles keep three thicknesses at ≥ 1:4.

#### Wood shingles (**Fig. 102**)
- Western red / white cedar heartwood (decay-resistant, low shrinkage), No. 1 and No. 2 grades; width **75–350 mm (3–14 in.)**; other species preservative-treated. Underlay/felt not usually required; eave protection required.
- First course **doubled**, upper overlapping joints, both rows projecting ~**25 mm (1 in.) beyond fascia** (figure: 12 mm / ½ in. for drip). **6 mm (¼ in.) gap** between shingles; joints offset **≥ 40 mm** from joints in course below and not aligned with the two previous courses.
- **Two nails per shingle**, at exposure + 40 mm from butt (e.g. 125 mm exposure → nail at 165 mm), **20 mm edge distance**; hot-dip galvanized/corrosion-resistant. Flat-grain shingles > 200 mm wide may be split and nailed as two.
- Fig. 102 labels: eave protection ≥ 300 mm beyond inside face of wall, roof sheathing, two nails per shingle, 20 mm edge distance, wood shingles, exposure, 40 mm lap, 6 mm space, fascia board, first course (double), project shingles 12 mm for drip.

#### Shakes (**Fig. 103**)
- Cedar hand-split: **length ≥ 450 mm (18 in.), width 100–350 mm (4–13¾ in.), butt 9–32 mm (⅜–1¼ in.)**. Min pitch **1:3**.
- Over spaced or closed sheathing; spaced: 19 × 89 mm (1 × 4) or wider strips on centres = exposure, never > 250 mm (10 in.); closed recommended where wind-driven snow.
- Exposure **190 mm (7½ in.) for 450 mm shakes, 250 mm (10 in.) for 600 mm (24 in.) shakes**.
- 900 mm (36 in.) No. 15 felt at eave line; starter course doubled (tripled for texture), bottom course 380 or 450 mm shakes. After each course, 450 mm (18 in.) No. 15 felt strip over top portion, bottom edge at **2 × exposure above butts** (e.g. 600 mm shakes @ 250 mm → felt 500 mm above butts, covering top 100 mm of shakes and ~350 mm onto sheathing). Gap **6–9 mm**; side joints offset ≥ 40 mm; froe-end (smoother) uppermost.

#### Finish at ridge and hips (**Fig. 104**)
- Asphalt: shingle squares (⅓ strip) over ridge/hip, blind-nailed, lapped to same coverage; orient cap away from prevailing wind. Wood: 150 mm (6 in.) wide shingles alternately lapped and blind-nailed, over No. 15 felt; flashing sometimes under wood ridge.

#### Built-up roofs (**Fig. 105**)
- Specialist installers; ≥ 3 layers of felt each sealed with tar or asphalt; gravel or cap sheet as ballast/UV protection. Coal tar and asphalt products incompatible.
- Eave trimmed with metal edging/flashing; gravel stop or cant strip with flashing. At walls: mopped to cant strip, turned up ≥ 150 mm (6 in.), sheathing paper and siding lapped over (50 mm min lap). Masonry-clad wall: membrane turned up, flashing over, counter-flashing embedded ≥ 25 mm in mortar, down ~150 mm, lapping ≥ 100 mm. Single-ply membranes also usable. Fig. 105 labels: siding, sheathing membrane, 50 mm minimum lap, membrane flashing, cant strip, roof sheathing, built-up roofing, metal gravel stop, fascia board.

#### Sheet metal roofing (**Fig. 106**)
- Widths **762–914 mm (30–36 in.)**, any length. Min slope **1:4** unless manufacturer proves lower. Over spaced supports: sheets designed for snow load, support under each end joint. Min thickness: 0.33 mm galvanized steel, 0.46 mm copper/zinc, 0.48 mm aluminum. Fig. 106 accessories: nailing strips for sheet metal roofing, eave starter, ridge cap, end wall flashing, valley, cottage hip, side wall flashing.

#### Concrete and clay tile roofing
- Considerably heavier; roof structure engineered for the additional load.

### Sustainable housing insight — Ch. 1

88	
89	## Roof slope conventions (p. 118–119)
90	
91	- Slope = rise-to-run ratio, **rise always first**. Two conventions:
92	  - **Imperial:** run always 12 (framing square). 45° = 12/12; 4/12 = 4 in. rise per 12 in. run.
93	  - **Ratio:** for slopes < 45° the *first* number (vertical) is 1 (e.g. 1:5 = 1 vertical per 5 horizontal); for slopes > 45° the *second* number (horizontal) is 1 (e.g. 5:1). Avoid mixed units (1 mm in 10 m).
94	  - 4/12 ≡ 1:3. Angular expressions acceptable where high accuracy needed.
95	- Pitched roofs vary from **1:6 to 1:1 or more**. Minimum slope for asphalt shingles is 1:6; different installation rules for ≥ 1:3 and < 1:3.
96	- Roof must have water-shedding surface, air and vapour barriers, thermal insulation and ventilation. Most Canadian houses: prefabricated trusses + unheated ventilated attic. Cathedral ceilings and flat roofs still need a vented space above insulation.
97	- Roof joist/rafter sizes by species/grade/live load: Tables 29–32 (pp. 295–301, not in excerpt).
98	
99	---
100	
101	## Chapter 11 — Ceiling and Roof Framing
102	
103	### Pitched roofs (p. 119)
104	- Prefabricated trusses most often used; site-framed rafters sometimes. **Gable roof is simplest**; hip or L-shape roofs can also be trussed (**Fig. 77**: L-shape trussed roof — plan with hatched roof planes and a valley; isometric shows ridge, valley trusses, roof sheathing, gable end, girder truss, common trusses, double wall plates).
105	
106	### Prefabricated roof trusses (pp. 119–122)
107	- Advantages: designed for local snow loads, quality control, less lumber waste, faster enclosure; provide surface for sheathing and ceiling, space for insulation.
108	- **Raised heel trusses** (**Fig. 78**) used in most new houses — deeper space at the eaves for insulation; truss anchors as requested by manufacturer/code. Energy codes lead to vertical depth ≥ 300 mm (12 in.) at outer face of exterior wall for trusses, rafters and roof joists.
109	- Trusses typically span exterior wall to exterior wall, no intermediate bearing → partitions placed freely; continuous air barrier/vapour retarder applied to underside before partitions.
110	- **Fig. 79 — Types of prefabricated roof trusses:** king-post · Howe · Fink or W · mono-pitch · parallel chord · scissor truss · mansard.
111	- Storage flat and clean; spans < 6 m (20 ft) installed by hand, longer need lifting equipment. Lift vertically to avoid lateral bending.
112	- Erection: gable truss first, braced to ground and wall; each additional truss generally **600 mm (24 in.) o.c.**, toe-nailed to top plates, temporarily braced (**Fig. 80** — gable ends normally sheathed before end braces). Then permanent bracing (**Fig. 81**): (a) top chord plane, (b) lateral web bracing, (c) web/bottom chord plane. Plan view: lateral braces across top chords, diagonal brace nailed to web repeated at ~6 m (20 ft); end elevation: 38 × 89 mm web bracing; side elevation: sheathing, blocking, lateral brace, diagonal braced bay at both ends and ~6 m intervals. Sheathing adds stiffness. Do not cut or alter trusses.
113	
114	### Site assembly of pitched roofs (pp. 122–127)
115	
116	**Fig. 82 — Types of pitched roofs:** Flat · Monopitch · Gable · Hip · Gambrel · Mansard.
117	
118	- Gable roof: rafters/trusses same length and pattern. Dormers add light/headroom (Fig. 88). **Hip roof: common rafters fastened to a ridge board, hip rafters supporting the jack rafters (Fig. 83B).**
119	- Liveable attics need insulation, air barrier, vapour barrier; framing may need to be upsized for insulation depth.
120	- **Ceiling joists** support ceiling finish and act as ties between exterior walls / opposing rafters; may carry loads from dwarf (knee) walls → size accordingly (Table 33); if they carry floor loads use floor joist tables (Tables 19, 20).
121	- Nail ceiling joists **after wall framing, before rafters** (rafter thrust otherwise pushes walls out). Joists tie lower ends of rafters in roofs sloping **≥ 1:3**; nail ceiling joist to side of each pair of rafters (**Fig. 83**).
122	- **Hip roofs:** where jack rafters run perpendicular to ceiling joists, a **stub joist** ties the jack rafter back to the ceiling joist (**Fig. 85**). Lap and nail joists or splice at centre bearing wall for a continuous tie. Nail counts depend on slope, spacing, snow load, house width (Table 24).
123	
124	**Fig. 83 — Roof framing and attachment**
125	- **A Gable roof:** ridge board, rafter, collar brace, collar tie, gable end stud, ceiling joist, top wall plate.
126	- **B Hip roof:** hip rafter **at least 50 mm (2 in.) deeper than jack rafters**, jack rafter, ceiling joist, top plate. Isometric: four hip rafters rising from the corners to a short ridge (shown as a vertical post marker at the apex in the drawing), jack rafters from plates to hips, common rafters from plates to ridge, ceiling joists spanning the short direction.
127	
128	- Dwarf walls perpendicular to ceiling joists (**Fig. 84**) add roof load; increase joist depth one size when slope > 1:4; when ≤ 1:4 use roof joist tables.
129	- **Fig. 84 — Rafter heel supported on a rafter plate:** rafter plate nailed to top of each ceiling joist with ≥ two 100 mm (4 in.) nails; rafter; ridge beam; exterior wall; knee wall with top and bottom plates and stud in line with each ceiling joist and rafter; struts at 1.2 m (4 ft) o.c.; ceiling joists lapped directly above interior load-bearing wall.
130	- Hip rafters ~51 mm (2 in.) deeper than common/jack rafters reduce space along end walls; in low-slope roofs the outside ceiling joist may not fit at normal spacing → **doubled joists** positioned to suit, then **tail joists** toenailed to outside wall plate and end-nailed to the doubled joist, at the same spacing as main joists (**Fig. 85**: jack rafter, hip rafter ≥ 50 mm deeper, ceiling joist, double ceiling joist, normal location for ceiling joist if space available, stub joist, end wall framing top plate).
131	- **Cutting rafters:** proper angle at ridge; **bird's mouth** notches at eaves; heel bears directly over exterior wall. Rafters placed: (a) directly on wall plates (Fig. 83); (b) on a rafter plate on the ceiling joists (Fig. 84); (c) on a load-bearing wall supported on the exterior wall plate (**Fig. 86**, used where part of the outside wall is inset — ceiling joists extend beyond exterior wall and are nailed to rafter sides).
132	- **Ridge board or ridge beam** ensures a level ridgeline. Erect rafters in pairs, nail to ridge, toe-nail lower ends to wall plate. Pairs directly opposite or **offset at ridge by ≤ their thickness** (offset needed when joists are lapped at the centre wall).
133	- **Slope < 1:3 → vertical support at peak:** 38 × 140 mm (2 × 6) ridge beam supported at 1.2 m (4 ft) by 38 × 89 mm (2 × 4) struts, or a load-bearing wall. Ridge support eliminates outward thrust → continuous ties unnecessary. Ridge beams also needed on steep roofs where rafter ends can't be tied.
134	- **Intermediate support** between ridge and exterior walls reduces rafter span (span measured from intermediate point to ridge/eave):
135	  - Slope ≥ 1:3: 38 × 89 mm **collar ties** nailed to each rafter pair; ties > 2.4 m (8 ft) braced against buckling with a 19 × 89 mm continuous member at right angles near centre (three 76 mm nails each end).
136	  - Slope < 1:3: **dwarf bearing wall** (Fig. 84), single top plate allowed if rafters over studs.
137	  - **Struts** 38 × 89 mm nailed to rafter side, bearing on load-bearing partition, **≥ 45° from horizontal** (Fig. 86).
138	  - Rafters perpendicular to ceiling joists: dwarf wall on a **beam between ceiling joists**, beam underside ≥ 25 mm (1 in.) above ceiling finish via blocks at bearing points.
139	  - Hip/valley rafters: beam with roof strut; or for a few rafters at a hip end a **"strongback"** of two 38 × 89 mm nailed on edge under the rafters, supported by 38 × 89 mm struts radiating from a common point on the interior bearing wall.
140	- **Hip and valley rafters ~50 mm (2 in.) deeper than common rafters** → full contact with the angle-cut of jack rafters (Figs. 83, 85, 87). Hip roof: jack rafters nailed to hip rafters and wall plate. Valley: jack rafters nailed to valley rafter and ridge.
141	- **Fig. 86 — Rafter heel supported on load-bearing wall:** ridge board; intermediate struts ≥ 45° to horizontal; 38 mm (2 in.) splice plate; interior bearing wall; rafters notched and bearing on top plate of exterior wall; continuous nailer and soffit supports; ceiling joists extend beyond exterior wall, nailed to rafters and toe-nailed to double wall plate; studs in load-bearing wall directly under each rafter; wall sheathing; exterior wall. Inset shows a house with an inset wall portion.
142	- **Fig. 87 — Framing at a valley:** valley rafter, jack rafter, common rafter, top plate, corner wall studs (inside corner of an L-plan: valley rafter rises from the inside corner; jack rafters from each wing's plate to the valley).
143	- **Dormers (Fig. 88):** rafters each side **doubled** to support side studs and valley rafters; top ends of valley rafters on a **double header** between the doubled rafters (joist hangers). Usual method: install roof sheathing first, frame dormer, cut sheathing flush with framing around opening; **bottom plate on top of the sheathing** supports side studs and is nailing base for wall sheathing. Size window for flashing/detailing.
144	
145	### Gable-end framing and projections (pp. 127–129)
146	- After roof framing, nail **gable-end studs**; in unfinished attics wide face may be parallel to wall; cut to rafter angle, toenail to plate and rafter underside with ≥ four 63 mm (2½ in.) nails each end.
147	- **Projection < 300 mm (12 in.)** (**Fig. 90 — Narrow projection**): **rake rafter** supported by ridge beam, rafter header, blocking and sheathing; 19 mm (¾ in.) nailing strip fastened to rafter above gable wall; blocking 600 mm (24 in.) o.c. toenailed to strip, end-nailed to rake rafter; soffit nailed to these, fascia added; gable wall sheathing taken up to underside of roof sheathing; rough fascia supports heel of rake rafter.
148	- **Projection > 300 mm (12 in.)** (**Fig. 89 — Wide projection supported by "lookout" rafters**): gable-end studs with narrow face parallel to sheathing + top wall plate; **lookouts** same size as rafters, **600 mm (24 in.) o.c.**, end-nailed to the first rafter inboard and to the gable top plate; blocking between lookouts at the wall line supports sheathing and inner soffit edge; **lookout length ≥ 2 × overhang**; **double rafter** where lookouts project > 1.5 rafter spaces into the roof. Labels: ridge beam, rafter, top plate of gable end wall, blocking between lookouts, lookouts 600 mm o.c., ceiling joist, top plate, header or rough fascia, fascia board at eave and gable end, corner studs.
149	
150	### Low-slope roofs (pp. 129–130)
151	- Must be more watertight (poorer drainage); may carry decks/traffic → durable materials.
152	- Rafters doubling as ceiling joists = **"roof joists"**, sized for roof + ceiling loads (Tables 29, 30); may need wider lumber / engineered wood for insulation and ventilation depth.
153	- Laid level or nearly level; **slope ≥ 1:50 for drainage** via ledger strip on bearing wall or tapered strip on joists.
154	- Overhang via **lookout rafters** (**Fig. 91**): if projecting > 1.5 joist spaces, two roof joists nailed together form a header; outside rafter header end-nailed to lookouts and joists (nailing for sheathing, fascia, soffit). Labels: alternative framing layout (dashed), roof joist, lookout rafter, header, exterior wall plate, rafter header.
155	
156	### Roof space ventilation (pp. 130–131)
157	- Always ventilate above insulation; membranes are vapour-resistant so vapour must be removed by ventilation.
158	- **Ice dams:** heat loss + sun melts roof snow, refreezes on cold eaves → water backs up (Fig. 100). Airtightness + insulation + ventilation keeps attic cold.
159	- Clearance between insulation and sheathing: **≥ 63 mm (2½ in.) without baffles, 25 mm (1 in.) with baffles**.
160	- **Vent area: ≥ 1/300 of insulated ceiling area for slopes ≥ 1:6; ≥ 1/150 for slopes < 1:6**; roof, gable or eave vents (**Fig. 92** soffit ventilation: baffle, perforated soffit, pre-finished fascia, airflow; **Fig. 93** ridge vent and gable vent). Uniformly distributed, ≥ 25% at bottom, ≥ 25% at top.
161	- Batt insulation between roof-ceiling joists (low slope): ≥ 63 mm vent space — achievable with **38 × 64 mm (2 × 3) cross-purlins** at right angles over joists (may be shimmed for slope). Rigid insulation above sheathing → no ventilation needed.
162	- Vents must exclude rain, snow, insects; baffle if moisture source; corrosion-resistant metal/plastic screens.
163	- **Attic access hatch ≥ 0.32 m² (3.4 sq ft), no dimension < 500 mm (20 in.)** except very small attics.
164	
165	### Worked sizing examples (pp. 132–134)
166	
167	| Example | Conditions | Selection |
168	|---|---|---|
169	| **Ceiling joists (Fig. 94)** | Inaccessible attic, no storage; ceiling carries insulation + drywall; span 4.3 m (14 ft 2 in.); spacing 400 mm (16 in.); SPF No. 2 and better | Table 33 → **38 × 140 mm (2 × 6)** |
170	| **Roof rafters (Fig. 95)** | Ottawa; snow load 1.72 kPa (36 psf); slope 1:3; rafter span 4.7 m (15 ft 6 in.); SPF No. 2; shingle roofing; lower ends restrained | Table 31 → **38 × 184 mm (2 × 8) at 300 mm o.c.** or **38 × 235 mm (2 × 10) at 600 mm o.c.** |
171	| **Roof joists (Fig. 96)** | Ottawa; 1.72 kPa; slope 1 in 3; roof joist span 4.19 m (13 ft 9 in.); SPF No. 2; shingles; lower ends restrained | Table 29 → **38 × 235 mm (2 × 10) at 400 mm o.c.** or **38 × 286 mm (2 × 12) at 600 mm o.c.** |
172	
173	Note (p. 132): National Building Code metric spacings are soft conversions — 12/16/24 in. → 300/400/600 mm; to suit 1220 × 2440 mm (4 × 8 ft) panels actual spacing is commonly **305/406/610 mm** o.c. Members must also be deep enough for required insulation.
174	
175	### Sustainable housing insight — Ch. 11 (p. 135)
176	- Energy: raised heel trusses / deep rafters for insulation over exterior walls; consider deeper members or closer spacing for future solar panels.
177	- Resource: trusses use select lumber + metal plates for long spans, less wood; suit local climate; fast; space for insulation/ventilation; all roof shapes; no site cut-offs.
178	- Affordability: plan attic conversion — stair location, size ceiling joists as floor joists, movable insulation, steeper slopes shed snow and enclose more attic volume, rough-in services.
179	
180	---
181	
182	## Chapter 12 — Roof Sheathing and Coverings
183	
184	### Roof sheathing (pp. 136–138)
185	- Sheathing-grade plywood, OSB or lumber planks over trusses/joists/rafters → nailing base for roofing + lateral bracing.
186	- **Panels (Fig. 97):** face grain **at right angles to framing**, joints offset (staggered), **2–3 mm (⅛ in.) gap**. Nails **150 mm (6 in.) o.c. minimum at edges, 300 mm (12 in.) o.c. intermediate**. Edge support: metal H-clips, 38 × 38 mm (2 × 2) blocking, or tongue-and-groove plywood. Thickness per Table 35 (depends on support spacing and edge support). Stagger fasteners at adjoining panel edges. Staples for 9.5 mm sheathing: 1.6 mm thick, 38.1 mm long, 9.5 mm crown, crown parallel to framing. Built-up roofing used as walking deck needs ≥ 15.5 mm (⅝ in.) sheathing.
187	- **Lumber boards (Fig. 98):** laid closed (edge to edge), ends supported, joints staggered. High wind/earthquake: laid **diagonally** or engineered. Usually 19 mm (¾ in.) thick; 17 mm allowed when supports ≤ 400 mm o.c. Boards ≤ 184 mm (8 in. nominal) wide: two 51 mm (2 in.) nails per bearing; wider: three; high wind: 63 mm nails. **No boards wider than 286 mm (12 in. nominal).** For wood shingle roofs boards may be **spaced** at the shingle exposure on centre (damp climates; lets shingles dry). Fig. 98 shows spaced method (nailing strips) above and closed method (roof boards, joint) below, on rafters/ceiling joists/plate.
188	- **Details (Fig. 99):** **50 mm (2 in.) clearance** of sheathing and framing from interior masonry/metal chimneys (12 mm / ½ in. for exterior masonry chimneys); header around opening; nail sheathing to rafters and headers. Fit sheathing tightly at **valleys and hips** and nail to valley/hip rafter → smooth base for flashing. Figure shows L-plan roof with valley, chimney opening with header, rafters, ridge board, ceiling joist, plate, stud.
189	
190	### Eave protection (pp. 138–140)
191	- Membrane along roof edge against water entry. **Not required** over unheated garages/porches, slope ≥ 1:1.5, or regions ≤ 3,500 heating degree-days.
192	- Extends **≥ 900 mm (36 in.) up the roof** (measured along slope) to **≥ 300 mm (12 in.) inside the inner face of the exterior wall** (horizontal). Installed under shingle starter course; usually self-adhering bituminous or roll roofing membrane (type S smooth or type M mineral-surfaced roll roofing, joints lapped ≥ 100 mm and cemented; or peel-and-stick).
193	- **Fig. 100 — Eave protection:** top: no protection — snow, trapped water backs up through membrane, thin ice slab under snow, melted snow running down underside of sheathing, ice in eavestrough; bottom: protection directs water off the roof. Prevent ice damming by air-sealing ceiling, ceiling/wall junction, penetrations; adequate insulation; eave venting. Keep skylights away from ice-dam areas.
194	
195	### Roof coverings (pp. 140–146)
196	- Install as soon as sheathing is on. Asphalt shingles common on pitched roofs; prefinished metal/galvanized steel/aluminum common in some regions (sheds snow); also roll roofing, wood shingles, shakes, sheet metal, concrete/clay tile; built-up with gravel/cap sheet for low slopes. Min/max slopes per covering in Table 36.
197	- **Minimum slopes: 1:6 asphalt shingles (low-slope application); 1:4 wood shingles; 1:3 hand-split shakes and asphalt shingles (normal application).**
198	
199	#### Asphalt shingles on slopes ≥ 1:3 (**Fig. 101**)
200	- Min No. 210 grade; square-butt strip **310 × 915 mm (12 × 36 in.)** or **335 × 1000 mm**, three tabs, exposure **130 mm (5 in.) or 145 mm (5¾ in.)**; 21–26 strips per bundle ≈ 3 m² (32 sq ft). Store flat; distribute bundles on roof.
201	- Sequence: eave protection → **starter strip** (shingles with tabs removed, or reversed shingles, or type M roll roofing) projecting ≥ 12 mm (½ in.) beyond eaves, rakes and fascia (drip edge; metal drip edges also ok), nailed 300 mm o.c. → first course with butt edge in line with bottom of starter strip → subsequent courses at allowed exposure (depends on slope, shingle type/length), aligned with chalk lines or underlay print lines.
202	- **Four large-head roofing nails per strip**, penetrating ≥ 12 mm into sheathing. Self-sealing tar seals. Fig. 101 labels: roof sheathing, eave protection, roofing nail, tar seals, exposure, fascia board, starting course.
203	
204	#### Asphalt shingles on low slopes 1:6 to 1:3
205	- Three thicknesses everywhere except first two courses, incl. hips and ridges; **exposure ≤ ⅓ shingle height**. Starter strips over a continuous cement band ≥ 200 mm (8 in.) wide; first course cemented with a band exposure + 100 mm (e.g. 250 mm for 150 mm exposure); subsequent courses band exposure + 50 mm (200 mm for 150 mm exposure); band 25–50 mm above butt edge to avoid defacing. Four fasteners above exposed portion. Cold cement ≈ 0.5 L/m², hot ≈ 1 kg/m². Only needed below 1:4 — special low-slope shingles keep three thicknesses at ≥ 1:4.
206	
207	#### Wood shingles (**Fig. 102**)
208	- Western red / white cedar heartwood (decay-resistant, low shrinkage), No. 1 and No. 2 grades; width **75–350 mm (3–14 in.)**; other species preservative-treated. Underlay/felt not usually required; eave protection required.
209	- First course **doubled**, upper overlapping joints, both rows projecting ~**25 mm (1 in.) beyond fascia** (figure: 12 mm / ½ in. for drip). **6 mm (¼ in.) gap** between shingles; joints offset **≥ 40 mm** from joints in course below and not aligned with the two previous courses.
210	- **Two nails per shingle**, at exposure + 40 mm from butt (e.g. 125 mm exposure → nail at 165 mm), **20 mm edge distance**; hot-dip galvanized/corrosion-resistant. Flat-grain shingles > 200 mm wide may be split and nailed as two.
211	- Fig. 102 labels: eave protection ≥ 300 mm beyond inside face of wall, roof sheathing, two nails per shingle, 20 mm edge distance, wood shingles, exposure, 40 mm lap, 6 mm space, fascia board, first course (double), project shingles 12 mm for drip.
212	
213	#### Shakes (**Fig. 103**)
214	- Cedar hand-split: **length ≥ 450 mm (18 in.), width 100–350 mm (4–13¾ in.), butt 9–32 mm (⅜–1¼ in.)**. Min pitch **1:3**.
215	- Over spaced or closed sheathing; spaced: 19 × 89 mm (1 × 4) or wider strips on centres = exposure, never > 250 mm (10 in.); closed recommended where wind-driven snow.
216	- Exposure **190 mm (7½ in.) for 450 mm shakes, 250 mm (10 in.) for 600 mm (24 in.) shakes**.
217	- 900 mm (36 in.) No. 15 felt at eave line; starter course doubled (tripled for texture), bottom course 380 or 450 mm shakes. After each course, 450 mm (18 in.) No. 15 felt strip over top portion, bottom edge at **2 × exposure above butts** (e.g. 600 mm shakes @ 250 mm → felt 500 mm above butts, covering top 100 mm of shakes and ~350 mm onto sheathing). Gap **6–9 mm**; side joints offset ≥ 40 mm; froe-end (smoother) uppermost.
218	
219	#### Finish at ridge and hips (**Fig. 104**)
220	- Asphalt: shingle squares (⅓ strip) over ridge/hip, blind-nailed, lapped to same coverage; orient cap away from prevailing wind. Wood: 150 mm (6 in.) wide shingles alternately lapped and blind-nailed, over No. 15 felt; flashing sometimes under wood ridge.
221	
222	#### Built-up roofs (**Fig. 105**)
223	- Specialist installers; ≥ 3 layers of felt each sealed with tar or asphalt; gravel or cap sheet as ballast/UV protection. Coal tar and asphalt products incompatible.
224	- Eave trimmed with metal edging/flashing; gravel stop or cant strip with flashing. At walls: mopped to cant strip, turned up ≥ 150 mm (6 in.), sheathing paper and siding lapped over (50 mm min lap). Masonry-clad wall: membrane turned up, flashing over, counter-flashing embedded ≥ 25 mm in mortar, down ~150 mm, lapping ≥ 100 mm. Single-ply membranes also usable. Fig. 105 labels: siding, sheathing membrane, 50 mm minimum lap, membrane flashing, cant strip, roof sheathing, built-up roofing, metal gravel stop, fascia board.
225	
226	#### Sheet metal roofing (**Fig. 106**)
227	- Widths **762–914 mm (30–36 in.)**, any length. Min slope **1:4** unless manufacturer proves lower. Over spaced supports: sheets designed for snow load, support under each end joint. Min thickness: 0.33 mm galvanized steel, 0.46 mm copper/zinc, 0.48 mm aluminum. Fig. 106 accessories: nailing strips for sheet metal roofing, eave starter, ridge cap, end wall flashing, valley, cottage hip, side wall flashing.
228	
229	#### Concrete and clay tile roofing
230	- Considerably heavier; roof structure engineered for the additional load.
231	
232	### Sustainable housing insight — Ch. 12 (p. 147)
233	- Deflect all water away from roof and walls; drip edges beyond materials below.
234	- Orient roof for future solar; finish service life ≥ renewable system; stiffer sheathing/closer framing for panels; building-integrated PV tiles.
235	- Make roof surface dimensions **multiples of 400 or 600 mm (16 or 24 in.)** to reduce panel waste; metal recyclable; wood renewable; keep roofs clear of leaves/branches to dry; concrete tile durable but heavy — extra framing/seismic reinforcement.
236	
237	---
238	
239	## Figure index
240	
241	| Fig. | Page | Title | Key content |
242	|---|---|---|---|
243	| 77 | 119 | L-shape trussed roof | Plan + isometric: ridge, valley trusses, girder truss, common trusses, gable end, double wall plates |
244	| 78 | 120 | Raised heel roof truss | Deeper eave for insulation; truss anchors |
245	| 79 | 120 | Types of prefabricated roof trusses | King-post, Howe, Fink/W, mono-pitch, parallel chord, scissor, mansard |
246	| 80 | 121 | Temporary bracing of roof trusses | Diagonal braces to ground/wall |
247	| 81 | 121 | Permanent bracing of roof trusses | Plan, end and side elevations; 6 m repeat |
248	| 82 | 122 | Types of pitched roofs | Flat, Monopitch, Gable, Hip, Gambrel, Mansard |
249	| 83 | 123 | Roof framing and attachment | A gable (ridge board, collar tie/brace, gable stud); B hip (hip rafter +50 mm, jack rafters) |
250	| 84 | 124 | Rafter heel on rafter plate | Rafter plate, knee wall, struts 1.2 m, lapped joists |
251	| 85 | 124 | Doubled ceiling joists and stub joists | Hip end framing near end wall |
252	| 86 | 125 | Rafter heel on load-bearing wall | Struts ≥ 45°, splice plate, inset wall |
253	| 87 | 126 | Framing at a valley | Valley rafter, jack rafter, common rafter, corner studs |
254	| 88 | 127 | Typical dormer framing | Double header, double rafter, valley rafter, side stud, sheathing first |
255	| 89 | 128 | Wide projection at gable end | Lookouts 600 mm o.c., blocking, rough fascia |
256	| 90 | 128 | Narrow projection at gable end | Rake rafter, 19 mm nailing strip, blocking 600 mm |
257	| 91 | 129 | Low-slope roof with overhang | Roof joist, lookout rafter, header, rafter header |
258	| 92 | 130 | Soffit roof ventilation | Baffle, perforated soffit, fascia |
259	| 93 | 131 | High-level roof ventilation | Ridge vent, gable vent |
260	| 94 | 132 | Ceiling joists | Example: span 4.3 m, spacing 400 mm |
261	| 95 | 133 | Roof rafters | Example: span 4.7 m, slope 1:3 |
262	| 96 | 134 | Roof joists | Example: span 4.19 m, slope 1:3 |
263	| 97 | 136 | Structural wood-panel roof sheathing | Grain ⊥ framing, 2–3 mm gap, nails 150/300 mm, H-clips |
264	| 98 | 137 | Wood-board roof sheathing | Spaced vs closed method |
265	| 99 | 138 | Sheathing at valley and chimney | 50 mm chimney clearance, header |
266	| 100 | 139 | Eave protection | Ice dam mechanism; 900 mm / 300 mm extents |
267	| 101 | 140 | Application of asphalt shingles | Starter course, exposure, nails, tar seals |
268	| 102 | 142 | Installation of wood shingles | Double first course, 6 mm gap, 40 mm lap, 2 nails |
269	| 103 | 143 | Installation of hand-split shakes | Dimensions, felt interlay, double starter |
270	| 104 | 144 | Finish at ridge and hips | Asphalt squares / wood 150 mm shingles, prevailing wind |
271	| 105 | 145 | Built-up roof | Cant strip, gravel stop, wall junction |
272	| 106 | 146 | Sheet metal roofing | Nailing strips, eave starter, ridge cap, valley, cottage hip, flashings |
273	
274	---
275	
276	## Summary for procedural modelling — hip roof framing sequence
277	
278	Members and rules for generating a site-framed hip roof (Figs. 82, 83B, 85, 87, 97–99):
279	
280	1. **Walls:** double top plates on exterior walls; studs/plates define the rectangular footprint. Optional interior load-bearing wall along the centre.
281	2. **Ceiling joists:** span the short direction at 400 or 600 mm o.c. (305/406/610 mm to suit panels), nailed to plates **before rafters**; lapped over the centre bearing wall. Typical 38 × 140 mm (2 × 6) for ~4.3 m span @ 400 mm. Near hip ends where the hip rafter leaves no room, use a **doubled joist** set inboard plus **stub/tail joists** to the end plate at the same spacing (Fig. 85).
282	3. **Ridge board:** level, centred on the short span; length = building length − building width (for equal-pitch hips, hip rafters meet the ridge ends at 45° in plan). Slope < 1:3 requires a ridge beam (38 × 140 mm) on 38 × 89 mm struts at 1.2 m, or a bearing wall.
283	4. **Common rafters:** from plates to ridge board in opposite pairs (or offset ≤ one thickness), bird's-mouth at the plate, heel bearing directly over the wall; depth ≥ 300 mm at wall face if insulation requires; spacing = joist spacing. Typical 38 × 184 mm @ 300 mm or 38 × 235 mm @ 600 mm for a 4.7 m span at 1:3 (Ottawa snow). Ceiling joist nailed to the side of each rafter.
284	5. **Hip rafters:** four, from each building corner to the ridge ends, at 45° in plan; **depth = common rafter depth + 50 mm (2 in.)**.
285	6. **Jack rafters:** from plates to hip rafters (hip jacks) on both the long and short sides, spacing continuing the common-rafter module, progressively shorter toward the corner, nailed to hip and plate.
286	7. **Valleys (L-plans):** valley rafter (also +50 mm deep) from the inside corner to the ridge; valley jacks from ridge to valley.
287	8. **Intermediate support if needed:** collar ties 38 × 89 mm on rafter pairs (slope ≥ 1:3), struts ≥ 45°, dwarf walls (slope < 1:3), strongback (2 × 38 × 89 mm) under hip-end jacks.
288	9. **Eaves/overhangs:** rafter tails project past the wall; fascia at rafter ends; soffit with perforated vent; gable-end overhangs (gable roofs only) via rake rafter (< 300 mm) or lookouts 600 mm o.c. (> 300 mm).
289	10. **Sheathing:** 1220 × 2440 mm panels, long dimension (face grain) perpendicular to rafters, staggered joints, 2–3 mm gaps, H-clips on unsupported edges, nails 150 mm edge / 300 mm field; trimmed tight at hips and valleys. Or 19 mm boards ≤ 286 mm wide, closed (edge to edge, joints staggered over supports) or spaced at the shingle exposure for wood shingles/shakes; diagonal in high wind/seismic areas.
290	11. **Covering:** eave protection 900 mm up slope; starter course; asphalt shingles (exposure 130/145 mm, ≥ 1:3) or wood shingles (exposure ~125 mm, ≥ 1:4) or shakes (exposure 190/250 mm, ≥ 1:3); ridge and hip caps lapped away from prevailing wind.
291	12. **Ventilation:** soffit intake + ridge/gable exhaust, ≥ 1/300 of ceiling area, 63 mm (or 25 mm with baffles) clear above insulation at eaves.
